source_text:
You know that moment when everyone's pulling out their phones to capture the sunset, and there's one person just watching it with their actual eyes? That person who says, I'm not on social media, and suddenly the whole room looks at them like they just confessed to living off the grid in a cave. Yeah, that person isn't a technophobe or a hermit. They might actually be protecting something most of us have already lost without even realizing it. If you're someone who genuinely has zero interest in scrolling through Instagram at 2 a.m., who doesn't feel the urge to document your coffee or share your thoughts with strangers, you're about to understand why your brain works differently from the 4.9 billion people currently glued to their screens. Here's what nobody tells you. In 2026, not using social media is essentially a radical act. Neuroscience is beginning to uncover something fascinating about people who choose this field. Their brains might be wired to resist something the rest of us fell for without question. Let's start with the obvious. Why does everyone else care so much? Social media taps into one of the most primitive parts of our brain, the need for social validation. When you post something and get likes, comments, shares, your brain releases dopamine, the same chemical that makes you crave chocolate, sex, and winning at video games. The platforms were literally designed by engineers who studied behavioral psychology to make them as addictive as possible. But here's where people who don't use social media get interesting. They're not immune to dopamine. They're just getting it from different sources. Research shows that their reward systems are less triggered by external validation and more activated by internal satisfaction. Translation? They don't need 200 strangers to like their vacation photo to feel like the vacation was worth taking. The experience itself is enough. Psychologists describe this as intrinsic versus extrinsic motivation. Most social media users are constantly seeking external validation to feel that their lives have meaning. People who avoid social media have figured out something crucial. They validate themselves. And once you can do that, the entire game changes. Now, there's a darker side to social media that many people are reluctant to acknowledge. It's not just about connection. It's about comparison. Every time you scroll, your brain is unconsciously measuring your life against everyone else's highlight reel. And you always lose that comparison because you're comparing your behind-the-scenes to everyone else's edited, filtered, perfectly curated performance. A study from the University of Pennsylvania found that limiting social media use to 30 minutes a day

significantly reduced depression and loneliness. But people who don't use it at all? They showed even lower rates of anxiety and higher levels of life satisfaction. Because they're not playing a game they can never win. They opted out entirely. Think about what happens to your attention span when you're constantly on social media. You're training your brain to crave quick hits of novelty every few seconds. Scroll, scroll, dopamine hit. Scroll, scroll, another hit. People who don't use social media have different attention spans. They can sit with one thought for more than 15 seconds. They can read a book without checking their phone every paragraph. There's actual brain imaging research on this. Heavy social media users show decreased activity in the prefrontal cortex, the part of your brain responsible for focus, decision-making, and impulse control. People who stay off social media train their attention span every single day. But let's be honest about something. Some people avoid social media for the wrong reasons. Not because they've made a conscious choice, but because they're hiding. Maybe they're scared of judgment, terrified of being seen. That's fear-based isolation, not intentional solitude. So here's the question you need to ask yourself. Are you avoiding it because it doesn't serve you or because you're afraid of what might happen if you showed up? Because one is empowerment. The other is self-protection masquerading as principle. For people who genuinely choose to stay off social media, there's something else happening. They've realized that social media isn't actually social. It's performance. Every post is a tiny audition for approval. Every story is a calculated move in an invisible game of status and perception. And people who opt out, they've looked at that game and said, this isn't a connection. This is theater. Real connection happens in three dimensions, not through a screen. It happens in the pause before someone answers a question, in the laugh that's too loud and unfiltered for a video, in the moment that's too ordinary to photograph, but somehow perfect anyway. People who don't use social media understand that the best moments in life are the ones you don't share. They're the ones you just live. Here's something wild that researchers discovered. People who don't use social media have stronger real-world relationships. Not more relationships, but deeper ones. Because they're not spreading their social energy across 500 acquaintances they haven't spoken to in a decade, they're investing it in the people who are actually in their lives. Quality.

Quality over quantity. Depth over breadth. And there's a time element here that's crucial. The average person spends over two and a half hours a day on social media. That's 912 hours a year. That's 38 full days of your life, every single year, scrolling through other people's lives instead of building your own. People who don't use social media, they get those 38 days back. And what do they do with them? They read. They create. They think. They exist without an audience. There's a concept in psychology called continuous partial attention. It's what happens when you're always half-present. One eye on the moment, one eye on your phone, waiting for the next notification. You're never fully anywhere. People who avoid social media have escaped that trap. When they're with you, they're actually with you. They aren't curating a sense of presence while mentally planning their next post. But society treats these people like aliens. You're not on Instagram? How do you keep in touch with people? As if humans didn't maintain relationships for thousands of years before social media existed. The truth is, people who don't use social media know something the rest of us are slowly learning the hard way. You don't need to broadcast your life to validate that it's worth living. You don't need an audience to make a moment meaningful. There's also a creativity angle here that's fascinating. Artists, writers, and creators who step away from social media consistently report something strange. Their work gets better. Instead of chasing algorithms, likes, and shares, they start creating for themselves again. The work becomes about expression, not performance. Social media has turned everyone into a personal brand, often without them even noticing. You're not just living your life, you're curating it, editing it, marketing it to an audience that's mostly bots and people who don't actually care. People who step away from social media leave that entire framework behind. They're not brands, they're just people. And there's a freedom in that. Most of us have forgotten exists. Let's talk about FOMO, the fear of missing out. It's the reason most people can't quit social media, even when they want to. But here's what people who don't use social media figured out. Most of what you're afraid of missing out on is completely meaningless. It's digital noise. And the things that actually matter, the real events, the genuine connections, those find you whether you're scrolling or not. Here's the uncomfortable truth about social media that nobody wants to say out loud. It's designed to make you feel inadequate, pulling you back in for validation. Every algorithm is optimized to show you content that triggers emotion, usually envy, outrage, or insecurity.

Because those emotions keep you engaged. People who don't use social media have removed themselves from a system specifically designed to make them feel not enough. And what happens when you're not constantly being told you're not enough? You begin to believe you're enough, just as you are. Without the perfect photo, the witty caption, the carefully constructed digital persona. You're free to exist, and that's revolutionary. There's also something to be said about memory and experience. Studies show that when you're constantly documenting moments for social media, you actually remember them less clearly. Because instead of experiencing the moment, you're thinking about how to frame it, caption it, share it. Your brain is in performance mode, not presence mode. People who don't use social media are building actual memories, not content. Now, before you think this is some anti-technology manifesto, it's not. Social media is a tool, but like any tool, you have to ask yourself, is this tool serving me, or am I serving it? People who don't use social media have answered that question honestly, and their answer was no. But here's what's important. This isn't about judgment. If social media genuinely adds value to your life, great. But be honest with yourself. Are you using it, or is it using you? Are you choosing to be there, or are you compulsively checking because your brain has been hijacked by an algorithm that profits from your attention? People who don't use social media aren't better than anyone else. They've just made a different choice. They've decided that their attention, their time, their mental energy, is worth more than whatever social media is offering in return. And in a world that's constantly trying to sell you convenience in exchange for your autonomy, that's a choice worth examining. If you're someone who doesn't use social media and people keep asking why, here's what you can tell them. Tell them you choose presence over productivity and experience life instead of documenting it. Or you can just smile and say, I tried it. It wasn't for me. Because honestly, you don't owe anyone an explanation for choosing to live your life on your own terms. The people who don't use social media are not missing out. They're just living differently. And maybe, just maybe, they're on to something the rest of us are too distracted to notice. Your attention is the most valuable thing you own. Every moment you spend scrolling is a moment you're giving away to someone else's agenda. People who stay off social media have figured that out. They've taken their attention back and they're spending it on things that actually matter to them. If they

If this resonates with you, just know this: you're not weird. You're not antisocial. You're not missing out on life. You're actually living it. And in a world where everyone's performing their existence for an audience that barely looks up from their own performance, that might be the most authentic thing you can do.
source_title: Psychology of People Who Don't Use Social Media

structure_splitter.prompt:
You are a structural analysis engine.

Your task is to split a long input text into logical blocks.

CRITICAL RULES:

— Do NOT rewrite the text  
— Do NOT summarize the text  
— Do NOT modify wording  
— Do NOT remove anything  
— Do NOT generate scenes  

You are ONLY splitting the text into blocks.

---

GOAL:

Split the text into meaningful logical blocks based on:

— topic shift  
— change of argument  
— new concept introduction  
— transition in narrative  
— change in emotional tone  

Each block must be:

— semantically coherent  
— internally complete  
— a full chunk of original text  

---

OUTPUT FORMAT:

Return ONLY a valid JSON array.

Each block must follow this structure:

{
  "block_id": number,
  "block_name": "short descriptive title",
  "purpose": "what this block does in the narrative",
  "text": "FULL original text of the block (unchanged)"
}

---

IMPORTANT:

— block_id must start from 1 and increment sequentially  
— blocks must NOT overlap  
— blocks must fully cover the entire text (no gaps, no missing parts)  
— ALL original text must be present inside blocks  

---

BLOCK SIZE RULES:

— Prefer blocks between 500–1000 characters  
— BUT prioritize meaning over size  
— A block can be shorter or longer if needed  

---

NAMING RULES:

block_name must be:

— short (3–6 words)  
— descriptive  
— reflect the core idea  

---

PURPOSE RULE:

purpose must explain:

— why this block exists  
— what role it plays  

---

STRICT TEXT RULE:

"text" field must:

— contain EXACT original text  
— preserve wording 1:1  
— preserve punctuation  
— preserve order  

NO paraphrasing  
NO rewriting  
NO compression  

---

DO NOT:

— output explanations  
— output markdown  
— output anything except JSON
structure_splitter.user_prompt:
Split the following text into logical structural blocks.

INPUT TEXT:
{{PASTE_FULL_TEXT}}

---

Additional requirements:

— detect natural topic shifts  
— do NOT split inside a continuous idea  
— avoid too many small blocks  
— avoid over-fragmentation  

Return ONLY JSON array.

structure.prompt:
Ты — YouTube Script Architect.

Твоя задача:
— взять готовый analysis.json
— построить сильную структуру будущего длинного YouTube-сценария
— разбить сценарий на логические блоки
— задать каждому блоку его роль, цель, длину и смысловые ограничения
— не писать сам сценарий
— не писать готовые абзацы
— не пересказывать исходный текст
— не заниматься стилистикой героя
— работать только как архитектор структуры

КРИТИЧЕСКИЕ ПРАВИЛА:

1. Не пиши сам текст блоков.
2. Не делай рерайт исходника.
3. Не делай слишком дробную структуру ради количества блоков.
4. Не делай микроблоки без самостоятельной смысловой функции.
5. Каждый блок должен двигать сценарий вперёд.
6. Вся структура должна ощущаться как единый narrative arc, а не как набор разрозненных тезисов.
7. Учитывай:
   — core_thesis
   — core_promise
   — key_ideas
   — facts_and_numbers
   — argument_flow
   — content_map A/B/C/D
   — weak_segments
   — retention_opportunities
   — donor_voice_signals
   — recommended_block_logic

ЧТО НУЖНО СДЕЛАТЬ:

1. Построй общую narrative_arc
Покажи, как должен развиваться ролик:
— с чего он начинается
— через какие смысловые фазы проходит
— к какому payoff приходит

2. Определи оптимальное количество блоков
Блоков должно быть столько, сколько реально нужно логике ролика.
Не дроби искусственно.
Не склеивай слишком крупно, если теряется управление.

3. Для каждого блока задай:

- block_id
- block_name
- block_role
- purpose
- target_chars_min
- target_chars_ideal
- target_chars_max
- must_cover
- must_not_cover
- source_mapping:
  - A
  - B
  - C
  - D
- hook_expectation:
  - opening_hook
  - mid_hooks
  - open_loop
- next_block_hint

4. Распредели длину по блокам так, чтобы:
— сумма target_chars_ideal примерно совпадала с target_chars_total
— важные блоки получали больше места
— второстепенные блоки не раздувались
— финал не был скомкан

5. Учитывай драматургию:
— сильный вход
— логическое развитие
— несколько точек усиления
— сильный финальный payoff

6. Учитывай будущего Block Writer:
Структура должна быть пригодна для поблочной генерации.
Каждый блок должен быть достаточно чётким, чтобы его можно было писать отдельно.

7. Учитывай donor_voice_signals:
Не закладывай в блоки:
— блогерский оффтоп
— личные ремарки донора
— обращения не по стилю
— шумовые вставки

8. Учитывай retention_opportunities:
Заранее вшивай в структуру места, где:
— нужен re-hook
— нужен contrast
— нужен stakes escalation
— нужен payoff pull

ФОРМАТ ВЫВОДА:

Верни строго JSON:

{
  "target_chars_total": <integer>,
  "narrative_arc": {
    "opening_function": "<string>",
    "middle_function": "<string>",
    "ending_function": "<string>",
    "arc_summary": "<string>"
  },
  "global_rules": {
    "language": "<string>",
    "voice_style": "for_voiceover",
    "avoid_repetition": true,
    "maintain_semantic_progression": true,
    "hook_density": "controlled",
    "tone_goal": "<string>"
  },
  "blocks": [
    {
      "block_id": <integer>,
      "block_name": "<string>",
      "block_role": "hook|setup|explanation|proof|contrast|turn|payoff|conclusion",
      "purpose": "<string>",
      "target_chars": <integer>,
      "must_cover": [
        "<string>"
      ],
      "must_not_cover": [
        "<string>"
      ],
      "source_mapping": {
        "A": ["<string>"],
        "B": ["<string>"],
        "C": ["<string>"],
        "D": ["<string>"]
      },
      "hook_expectation": {
        "opening_hook": <boolean>,
        "mid_hooks": <integer>,
        "open_loop": <boolean>
      },
      "next_block_hint": "<string>"
    }
  ]
}

analysis.prompt:
Ты — аналитический редактор YouTube-сценариев.

Твоя задача:
— глубоко разобрать исходный текст
— извлечь его смысловую структуру
— выделить факты, аргументы, идеи и слабые места
— подготовить структурированную аналитическую основу для дальнейшего построения нового сценария

КРИТИЧЕСКИЕ ПРАВИЛА:

1. Не пиши новый сценарий.
2. Не переписывай исходный текст.
3. Не делай краткий пересказ ради пересказа.
4. Не сокращай смысл агрессивно.
5. Не придумывай новых фактов.
6. Твоя задача — разбор, а не рерайт.

ЧТО НУЖНО СДЕЛАТЬ:

1. Определи core_thesis
Что является главным тезисом исходного текста?

2. Определи core_promise
Что зритель или читатель должен понять, почувствовать или усвоить к концу?

3. Выдели key_ideas
Разбей текст на ключевые смысловые идеи.
Не фразы, а именно логические единицы.

4. Выдели facts_and_numbers
Извлеки:
— числа
— статистику
— фактические утверждения
— исследования
— конкретные claims
Если точность важна, помечай это.

5. Построй argument_flow
Покажи, как именно движется логика текста:
— с чего начинается
— что доказывается
— через какие переходы
— к чему приходит

6. Найди weak_segments
Определи слабые места:
— повторы
— провисания
— оффтоп
— слабые переходы
— рыхлые объяснения
— лишние эмоциональные вставки
— части, не несущие ценности для нового сценария

7. Найди retention_opportunities
Определи места, где в будущем можно усилить удержание:
— где просится сильный хук
— где нужен re-hook
— где есть хороший потенциал для контраста
— где можно усилить payoff

8. Сделай классификацию A/B/C/D

A — preserve_exactly
Сюда относятся:
— числа
— статистика
— важные факты
— исследования
— точные формулировки, если они критичны

B — preserve_meaning
Сюда относятся:
— аргументы
— причинно-следственные связи
— логические цепочки
— ключевые объяснения

C — can_adapt
Сюда относятся:
— примеры
— метафоры
— аналогии
— второстепенные иллюстрации
— способы подачи

D — must_rewrite
Сюда относятся:
— хуки
— вступление
— переходы
— стиль
— обращения к аудитории
— чужая манера речи
— бытовые оффтоп-вставки

9. Определи donor_voice_signals
Найди признаки чужого голоса, которые нельзя тянуть в новый сценарий:
— обращения не по стилю
— лишняя блогерская бытовуха
— случайные личные вставки
— манера речи, не подходящая герою нового канала

10. Оцени narrative_value
Покажи, какие части текста реально несут ценность для построения сильного нового ролика, а какие — нет.

ВАЖНО:

— не пытайся сделать текст красивым
— не добавляй стилистику
— не пиши как сценарист
— пиши как аналитик структуры и смысла

ФОРМАТ ВЫВОДА:

Верни строго JSON следующего вида:

{
  "analysis_mode": "full_analysis",
  "core_thesis": "<string>",
  "core_promise": "<string>",
  "target_audience_in_source": "<string>",
  "content_type_in_source": "<string>",
  "key_ideas": [
    {
      "idea_id": "idea_01",
      "title": "<short title>",
      "description": "<meaningful explanation>"
    }
  ],
  "facts_and_numbers": [
    {
      "fact_id": "fact_01",

youtube_title: Psychology of People Who Don't Use Social Media
youtube_transcript_text:
You know that moment when everyone's pulling out their phones to capture the sunset, and there's one person just watching it with their actual eyes? That person who says, I'm not on social media, and suddenly the whole room looks at them like they just confessed to living off the grid in a cave. Yeah, that person isn't a technophobe or a hermit. They might actually be protecting something most of us have already lost without even realizing it. If you're someone who genuinely has zero interest in scrolling through Instagram at 2 a.m., who doesn't feel the urge to document your coffee or share your thoughts with strangers, you're about to understand why your brain works differently from the 4.9 billion people currently glued to their screens. Here's what nobody tells you. In 2026, not using social media is essentially a radical act. Neuroscience is beginning to uncover something fascinating about people who choose this field. Their brains might be wired to resist something the rest of us fell for without question. Let's start with the obvious. Why does everyone else care so much? Social media taps into one of the most primitive parts of our brain, the need for social validation. When you post something and get likes, comments, shares, your brain releases dopamine, the same chemical that makes you crave chocolate, sex, and winning at video games. The platforms were literally designed by engineers who studied behavioral psychology to make them as addictive as possible. But here's where people who don't use social media get interesting. They're not immune to dopamine. They're just getting it from different sources. Research shows that their reward systems are less triggered by external validation and more activated by internal satisfaction. Translation? They don't need 200 strangers to like their vacation photo to feel like the vacation was worth taking. The experience itself is enough. Psychologists describe this as intrinsic versus extrinsic motivation. Most social media users are constantly seeking external validation to feel that their lives have meaning. People who avoid social media have figured out something crucial. They validate themselves. And once you can do that, the entire game changes. Now, there's a darker side to social media that many people are reluctant to acknowledge. It's not just about connection. It's about comparison. Every time you scroll, your brain is unconsciously measuring your life against everyone else's highlight reel. And you always lose that comparison because you're comparing your behind-the-scenes to everyone else's edited, filtered, perfectly curated performance. A study from the University of Pennsylvania found that limiting social media use to 30 minutes a day

significantly reduced depression and loneliness. But people who don't use it at all? They showed even lower rates of anxiety and higher levels of life satisfaction. Because they're not playing a game they can never win. They opted out entirely. Think about what happens to your attention span when you're constantly on social media. You're training your brain to crave quick hits of novelty every few seconds. Scroll, scroll, dopamine hit. Scroll, scroll, another hit. People who don't use social media have different attention spans. They can sit with one thought for more than 15 seconds. They can read a book without checking their phone every paragraph. There's actual brain imaging research on this. Heavy social media users show decreased activity in the prefrontal cortex, the part of your brain responsible for focus, decision-making, and impulse control. People who stay off social media train their attention span every single day. But let's be honest about something. Some people avoid social media for the wrong reasons. Not because they've made a conscious choice, but because they're hiding. Maybe they're scared of judgment, terrified of being seen. That's fear-based isolation, not intentional solitude. So here's the question you need to ask yourself. Are you avoiding it because it doesn't serve you or because you're afraid of what might happen if you showed up? Because one is empowerment. The other is self-protection masquerading as principle. For people who genuinely choose to stay off social media, there's something else happening. They've realized that social media isn't actually social. It's performance. Every post is a tiny audition for approval. Every story is a calculated move in an invisible game of status and perception. And people who opt out, they've looked at that game and said, this isn't a connection. This is theater. Real connection happens in three dimensions, not through a screen. It happens in the pause before someone answers a question, in the laugh that's too loud and unfiltered for a video, in the moment that's too ordinary to photograph, but somehow perfect anyway. People who don't use social media understand that the best moments in life are the ones you don't share. They're the ones you just live. Here's something wild that researchers discovered. People who don't use social media have stronger real-world relationships. Not more relationships, but deeper ones. Because they're not spreading their social energy across 500 acquaintances they haven't spoken to in a decade, they're investing it in the people who are actually in their lives. Quality.

Quality over quantity. Depth over breadth. And there's a time element here that's crucial. The average person spends over two and a half hours a day on social media. That's 912 hours a year. That's 38 full days of your life, every single year, scrolling through other people's lives instead of building your own. People who don't use social media, they get those 38 days back. And what do they do with them? They read. They create. They think. They exist without an audience. There's a concept in psychology called continuous partial attention. It's what happens when you're always half-present. One eye on the moment, one eye on your phone, waiting for the next notification. You're never fully anywhere. People who avoid social media have escaped that trap. When they're with you, they're actually with you. They aren't curating a sense of presence while mentally planning their next post. But society treats these people like aliens. You're not on Instagram? How do you keep in touch with people? As if humans didn't maintain relationships for thousands of years before social media existed. The truth is, people who don't use social media know something the rest of us are slowly learning the hard way. You don't need to broadcast your life to validate that it's worth living. You don't need an audience to make a moment meaningful. There's also a creativity angle here that's fascinating. Artists, writers, and creators who step away from social media consistently report something strange. Their work gets better. Instead of chasing algorithms, likes, and shares, they start creating for themselves again. The work becomes about expression, not performance. Social media has turned everyone into a personal brand, often without them even noticing. You're not just living your life, you're curating it, editing it, marketing it to an audience that's mostly bots and people who don't actually care. People who step away from social media leave that entire framework behind. They're not brands, they're just people. And there's a freedom in that. Most of us have forgotten exists. Let's talk about FOMO, the fear of missing out. It's the reason most people can't quit social media, even when they want to. But here's what people who don't use social media figured out. Most of what you're afraid of missing out on is completely meaningless. It's digital noise. And the things that actually matter, the real events, the genuine connections, those find you whether you're scrolling or not. Here's the uncomfortable truth about social media that nobody wants to say out loud. It's designed to make you feel inadequate, pulling you back in for validation. Every algorithm is optimized to show you content that triggers emotion, usually envy, outrage, or insecurity.

Because those emotions keep you engaged. People who don't use social media have removed themselves from a system specifically designed to make them feel not enough. And what happens when you're not constantly being told you're not enough? You begin to believe you're enough, just as you are. Without the perfect photo, the witty caption, the carefully constructed digital persona. You're free to exist, and that's revolutionary. There's also something to be said about memory and experience. Studies show that when you're constantly documenting moments for social media, you actually remember them less clearly. Because instead of experiencing the moment, you're thinking about how to frame it, caption it, share it. Your brain is in performance mode, not presence mode. People who don't use social media are building actual memories, not content. Now, before you think this is some anti-technology manifesto, it's not. Social media is a tool, but like any tool, you have to ask yourself, is this tool serving me, or am I serving it? People who don't use social media have answered that question honestly, and their answer was no. But here's what's important. This isn't about judgment. If social media genuinely adds value to your life, great. But be honest with yourself. Are you using it, or is it using you? Are you choosing to be there, or are you compulsively checking because your brain has been hijacked by an algorithm that profits from your attention? People who don't use social media aren't better than anyone else. They've just made a different choice. They've decided that their attention, their time, their mental energy, is worth more than whatever social media is offering in return. And in a world that's constantly trying to sell you convenience in exchange for your autonomy, that's a choice worth examining. If you're someone who doesn't use social media and people keep asking why, here's what you can tell them. Tell them you choose presence over productivity and experience life instead of documenting it. Or you can just smile and say, I tried it. It wasn't for me. Because honestly, you don't owe anyone an explanation for choosing to live your life on your own terms. The people who don't use social media are not missing out. They're just living differently. And maybe, just maybe, they're on to something the rest of us are too distracted to notice. Your attention is the most valuable thing you own. Every moment you spend scrolling is a moment you're giving away to someone else's agenda. People who stay off social media have figured that out. They've taken their attention back and they're spending it on things that actually matter to them. If they

If this resonates with you, just know this: you're not weird. You're not antisocial. You're not missing out on life. You're actually living it. And in a world where everyone's performing their existence for an audience that barely looks up from their own performance, that might be the most authentic thing you can do.
